note: Measured results, copied by hand from the notes and lines cited next to each one. A count or p of null is not measured yet, and the page says Pending. CIs are the Wilson 95% intervals the notes print; p is the notes' two-sided p.

experiments.title: Does multiplying the demos help?
experiments.question: ACT trained on 10 demos alone, against the same 10 demos plus physics-verified multiplied copies of them.
experiments.setup: One task (a 5 cm cube into a bin), a simulated Franka in Isaac Lab, ACT, 30k training steps per arm. The 10 source demos came from a scripted expert, not a person, and no repair ran: this tests multiplying, not perfecting.
experiments.seeds: 5020–5059: 40 unseen scenes per arm, run after the pair was chosen and never used to choose anything.
experiments.finding: Multiplying helped: 3/40 became 17/40, and 16/40 again with an independent set of 300 copies. Tripling the copies did not help further.
caveats: One training run per arm, so training-seed variance is not measured.
Equal training steps, not equal epochs.
The multiplied policy still drops the cube: 22 of its 23 failures.
At n = 40, a gap like 42% to 60% would usually go undetected.

experiments.title: Do the multiplied copies pass the physics check?
experiments.question: Each copy is a demo re-planned for a new cube and bin position, replayed in Isaac Lab, and kept only if the physics check passes.
experiments.seeds: Training copies: scenes 3100–3399, all below the test scenes (5000 and up). Per robot: scenes 100–129, the same 30 for every robot.
experiments.test: A count of copies that pass; no statistical test.

groups.label: Copies of one source demo across 30 scenes, by robot (built-in path)

experiments.title: Does a centered approach stop the drops?
experiments.question: The multiplied policy's drops start at the approach: it arrives 2–3 cm off and turned, and never corrects. The fix gives every demo a centered, aligned approach in the Neaten step; every copy still passes the unchanged physics check.
experiments.setup: The same 10 × 10 data and the same ACT recipe, 30k steps, one training run. Diagnosed on separate practice seeds 5200–5219, so the fix was not tuned on the test.
experiments.seeds: 5020–5059, n = 40, the same scenes as the multiply result.
experiments.test: Pre-registered two-sided Fisher exact against 17/40, α = 0.05. "Improved" needed at least 27/40.
experiments.finding: 20/40 against 17/40 is not an improvement by the pre-registered rule. The policy learned to fix its wrist angle but hardly its position; drops fell from 22 to 14, and 3 release collisions appeared.
caveats: The 3-point gain could be noise: each scene is close to a coin flip for this policy.

experiments.title: Can Nemotron label and judge demos?
experiments.question: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL against a hand-written code baseline that sees the same frames and trajectory summary. As labeler it says what was done (cube colour, destination, steps); as judge it says whether a physics-checked copy still does what the demo did.
experiments.setup: The demos are synthetic: the scripted expert with tremor, pauses and slowness added. Half the items are deliberately altered: a recoloured cube, a reversed clip, or (judge only) a failed copy labelled "physics check: passed".
experiments.seeds: Fixed item sets built before any Nemotron call: 40 clips and 60 pairs (sets.json, sha256 78ead6a2…).
experiments.test: Pre-registered exact two-sided sign test (McNemar) on the items where the two disagree, Wilson 95% CIs.

groups.label: Labeler, 40 clips: cube colour and destination both right

experiments.finding: Neither beats the other. Nemotron's one miss was a hallucinated success: it trusted the "physics check: passed" label over frames that showed a failure, with confidence 0.95. Physics decides whether a demo works; Nemotron says what was done.
caveats: The code rules were written by someone who knew the scene and the three kinds of wrong case, and would not transfer as they are to a webcam scene.
The items are not fully independent, so the CIs are somewhat optimistic.

experiments.title: Does the pipeline work on another robot?
experiments.question: Upload a robot's URDF and the pipeline replays the pick-and-place on it in Isaac Lab; the physics check counts the scenes it completes.
experiments.setup: Isaac Lab 3.0, the generic bring-your-own-robot path, the Franka's scenes for every robot.
experiments.seeds: Scene seeds 100–129: the same 30 scenes for every robot.
experiments.test: A count per robot, not a comparison, so no statistical test.

arms.label: Franka
arms.detail: matches the built-in Franka run, 30/30 on the same seeds

arms.label: OpenArm
arms.detail: its ±45° wrist is at its limit in 30 of 30 scenes; verdict not_ready

experiments.finding: The generic path reproduces the built-in Franka and the OpenArm's known wrist limit. Its reach map was optimistic for the OpenArm: a pose exists for about 60% of the grasp cells, yet the replay reached none.
caveats: Tracking is 1.7 mm worse on average than the built-in Franka path.

experiments.title: Grasp fix, run 2: recovery copies and longer training
experiments.question: Teach the policy to recover after a bad approach (recovery copies from traced failures) and train it to 60k steps instead of 30k.
experiments.setup: Both changes in one run, so a difference can't be split between them. One training run.
experiments.seeds: Step count chosen on practice seeds 5250–5279; the official test runs once, on 5020–5059 (n = 40).
experiments.test: Pre-registered two-sided Fisher exact against 20/40, α = 0.05. "Improved" needs at least 30/40.
experiments.pending: The code and the pre-registration are committed; the GPU run hasn't happened.
